before: A package manifest describes buildable targets and products. Here one executable target depends on a library target inside the same package; no external package is fetched.

Use an existing Swift 6.0-or-newer command-line toolchain and a new empty local directory for each variant. These are complete local files, not one source file for the app’s Run button. Actual recorded execution is Swift 6.4.1/Linux in language mode 6, not a Mac/Xcode or compiler 6.0 verification. No registry package, network service or user-machine installation is needed. Commands below assume a shell with swift/swiftc on PATH; preserve paths and run from that directory. Package.swift begins with the tools-version declaration, which sets the manifest/toolchain requirement; it is not proof of behavior on every Swift 6 compiler. import PackageDescription exposes Package and target/product factory APIs. Package(name:products:targets:) builds the manifest description. .library and .executable declare exported products from target names. .target declares the library; .executableTarget declares the command-line program and its intra-package dependency. Target names match their Sources subdirectories. public routeName(_:) takes a place and returns prefixed text; the executable imports TrailKit to call it. swift build builds this package. swift run --skip-build TrailDemo runs the product already built; it does not compile a missing build.

File `Package.swift`:
```swift
// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription
let package = Package(
    name: "TrailStudy",
    products: [
        .library(name: "TrailKit", targets: ["TrailKit"]),
        .executable(name: "TrailDemo", targets: ["TrailDemo"])
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "TrailKit"),
        .executableTarget(name: "TrailDemo", dependencies: ["TrailKit"])
    ]
)
```

File `Sources/TrailKit/Route.swift`:
```swift
public func routeName(_ place: String) -> String {
    return "Route:" + place
}
```

File `Sources/TrailDemo/main.swift`:
```swift
import TrailKit
print(routeName("Lake"))
```

Run these local commands in order:
```sh
swift build
swift run --skip-build TrailDemo
```
Build succeeds without an external dependency. The run command prints exactly `Route:Lake` followed by a newline. Build progress text and paths are not stable output contracts.

after: A package is a group of related code. A target is one part the build tools can compile. This example has a library target, TrailKit, and a program target, TrailDemo, that uses it. Use a new empty folder and an existing Swift 6-compatible command-line toolchain.

Create Package.swift at the top of that folder:
```swift
// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription
let package = Package(
    name: "TrailStudy",
    products: [
        .library(name: "TrailKit", targets: ["TrailKit"]),
        .executable(name: "TrailDemo", targets: ["TrailDemo"])
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "TrailKit"),
        .executableTarget(name: "TrailDemo", dependencies: ["TrailKit"])
    ]
)
```
This file is the manifest: the package's build plan. products names the library and program people can use. targets defines their code. dependencies says TrailDemo needs TrailKit. The first line declares the minimum tools version.

Create Sources/TrailKit/Route.swift:
```swift
public func routeName(_ place: String) -> String {
    return "Route:" + place
}
```
The folder name matches the TrailKit target. public lets the other target call routeName. The function adds Route: before the supplied place.

Create Sources/TrailDemo/main.swift:
```swift
import TrailKit
print(routeName("Lake"))
```
The folder name matches TrailDemo. import TrailKit makes the library available, so the program can call routeName with Lake.

From the folder containing Package.swift, run:
```sh
swift build
swift run --skip-build TrailDemo
```
Build must succeed before using --skip-build. The program should print Route:Lake. TrailKit is another target in this same package, so this example does not download an outside package.
